q: Ruth, 44, asks how much life insurance she needs. Her debts total $300,000. Income replacement for her family is estimated at $900,000. Education funding needs are $200,000 and final expenses $30,000. She has $500,000 of existing life insurance and $150,000 of liquid savings. Using a needs-based approach, which amount best represents her remaining need?
choices: $1,430,000, because a needs analysis does not subtract existing resources
$650,000, because liquid savings are subtracted twice
$930,000, because existing life insurance is subtracted and liquid savings are ignored
$780,000, because existing insurance and liquid savings both offset the total need
rationale: Wrong — a needs analysis always offsets existing resources; leaving them out overstates the need.
Wrong — liquid savings are counted once, and this result double-subtracts them.
Wrong — this subtracts only the life insurance; the $150,000 of liquid savings also reduces the need.
Correct — total needs of $1,430,000 less $500,000 of insurance and $150,000 of savings leaves $780,000.
explanation: Needs approach: add all capital needs, then subtract existing life insurance and liquid assets earmarked for those needs.

q: A policyowner misses a premium. The policy is in its 31-day grace period. The insured dies during the grace period. Which statement is correct?
choices: The death benefit is payable, reduced by the overdue premium
The beneficiary must pay the missed premium before any benefit is paid
The policy is void, and no death benefit is payable
The full death benefit is payable, with no reduction
rationale: Correct — during the grace period coverage continues, and the unpaid premium is subtracted from the death benefit.
Wrong — the beneficiary is not required to pay the premium as a condition of the claim.
Wrong — coverage remains in force during the grace period, so the claim is not void for nonpayment.
Wrong — the overdue premium is deducted from the proceeds in the usual case.
explanation: A grace period keeps coverage in force; the death benefit is reduced by any premium due.

q: A life insurance policy was issued 18 months ago. The insured dies by suicide. The policy has a standard two-year suicide provision. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: No benefit is payable, because suicide is always excluded for life
The insurer generally pays only the premiums paid, since the claim falls within the suicide provision period
The benefit is payable in full, because the policy was in force for more than one year
The full face amount is payable, because the exclusion applies only to accidental deaths
rationale: Wrong — the standard suicide provision is time-limited (commonly two years), so it does not exclude suicide for life.
Correct — within the suicide provision period, most policies limit the payout to premiums paid.
Wrong — one year is not the standard threshold; the claim falls inside the typical two-year period.
Wrong — the suicide provision applies to suicide, not to accidents; accidental death is not the issue here.
explanation: Standard suicide provisions exclude or limit benefits for a set early period, commonly two years, and then the full benefit applies.

q: A policy was issued four years ago. The insurer learns the insured understated her smoking history on the application. She dies today from an unrelated cause. The policy is past its two-year contestable period. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The insurer may void the policy and refund only the premiums paid
The insurer may deny the claim, because misrepresentation can be raised at any time
The insurer generally cannot deny the claim for the misstatement, though it may adjust the benefit to what the premiums would have bought at the correct rate
The insurer must pay the claim in full, and the misstatement can never affect the benefit
rationale: Wrong — rescission is generally limited to the contestable period, so a refund of premiums is not the typical remedy here.
Wrong — after the contestability period, most states limit the insurer's ability to deny for misstatements, except for fraud.
Correct — after the contestability period, the usual remedy for a misstatement of health is an adjustment to the benefit, not rescission.
Wrong — a misstatement can still affect the amount payable, and fraud can change the outcome.
explanation: Incontestability generally bars rescission after two years; misstatements of age or sex usually adjust the benefit, and fraud is an exception in most states.

q: A surgeon is disabled and can no longer operate, but she can teach and consult. Her policy is an own-occupation policy with a residual benefit rider. Which best describes the likely outcome?
choices: The policy pays only after she has been out of work for ten years
No benefit is payable, because she can still work in some capacity
The full benefit is payable, because own-occupation coverage pays the full benefit in every case
A proportional residual benefit is payable, based on the income loss, under the rider's terms
rationale: Wrong — no standard policy requires a ten-year wait for a residual benefit.
Wrong — the residual rider exists specifically to pay partial benefits when a person can still work at reduced earnings.
Wrong — own-occupation pays the full benefit only when the insured cannot perform her own occupation; here she can still partly work, so the residual rider matters.
Correct — the residual benefit pays a proportion of the full benefit that matches the percentage of income lost, if the rider's trigger is met.
explanation: Residual riders pay a proportional benefit when earnings fall below a defined threshold because of disability.

q: A dental practice owner wants insurance to keep the office running during a disability, including rent, payroll, and equipment leases, but not his personal living costs. Which coverage best fits?
choices: Business overhead expense insurance
Key person life insurance on the owner
Long-term care insurance for the owner
Individual disability income insurance on the owner
rationale: Correct — business overhead expense insurance reimburses ordinary fixed business expenses while the owner is disabled.
Wrong — key person life pays on death, not on disability, so it does not cover the practice's expenses during a disability.
Wrong — long-term care pays for care services and does not fund business operating costs.
Wrong — individual disability income replaces the owner's personal income, not the practice's fixed costs.
explanation: Business overhead expense (BOE) pays the business's fixed operating costs during disability. Personal disability income covers the owner's own paycheck.

q: A homeowner's roof is destroyed by hail. Her HO-3 policy is written on a replacement cost basis. Which statement about payment is most accurate?
choices: Replacement cost policies pay the full replacement cost immediately, with no holdback
Replacement cost policies typically pay actual cash value first and the balance of the replacement cost after repair or replacement is completed
Replacement cost policies pay only the market value of the home
Replacement cost policies never pay for hail damage
rationale: Wrong — most replacement cost policies hold back the depreciation until repairs are finished.
Correct — the insurer typically pays actual cash value first, then the recoverable depreciation once the work is complete.
Wrong — replacement cost is based on rebuilding or replacing the damaged property, not on market value.
Wrong — hail is a covered peril under a standard HO-3 for the dwelling, subject to the policy's terms.
explanation: Replacement cost policies pay ACV up front and the depreciation holdback after the repair is completed, subject to policy terms.

q: A client has auto liability limits of $250,000 per person and $500,000 per accident, and a homeowners liability limit of $300,000. He buys a $1,000,000 umbrella policy. In a serious at-fault accident, the total judgment is $1,200,000 and the underlying limits are fully used. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The umbrella pays only if the underlying policies were canceled
The umbrella pays the entire $1,200,000 and the underlying policies pay nothing
The umbrella pays the excess above the underlying limits, subject to its own terms and exclusions
The umbrella replaces the underlying policies, so the client pays nothing at all
rationale: Wrong — the umbrella is designed to apply on top of active underlying policies, not after they are canceled.
Wrong — the underlying auto policy pays up to its own limit first; the umbrella does not replace it.
Correct — the umbrella responds above the required underlying limits, subject to its own exclusions and conditions.
Wrong — an umbrella supplements underlying coverage and does not eliminate the need for it.
explanation: Umbrella coverage is excess liability: it pays after the required underlying limits are exhausted, under its own terms.

sub: Health insurance and health care cost management (individual and group)
q: Ben, 66, has been contributing to an HSA through his employer's high-deductible plan. He enrolls in Medicare Part A and Part B this month. Which statement is correct?
choices: He may contribute up to the family limit because he is now a Medicare beneficiary
He may keep contributing to the HSA as long as he remains in the high-deductible plan
He may contribute only the employer's share, and his own contributions must stop
He can no longer make HSA contributions once he is enrolled in any part of Medicare
rationale: Wrong — Medicare enrollment does not increase the contribution limit; it ends eligibility.
Wrong — enrollment in any part of Medicare ends HSA eligibility, even while still in the high-deductible plan.
Wrong — the rule is not split between employer and employee contributions; enrollment in Medicare ends HSA eligibility.
Correct — enrollment in any part of Medicare makes a person ineligible to contribute to an HSA going forward.
explanation: HSA eligibility requires HDHP coverage and no enrollment in Medicare. Contributions stop once Medicare begins, though existing funds remain usable.

sub: Health insurance and health care cost management (individual and group)
q: A client was laid off and lost employer group health coverage. She elects COBRA continuation. Under the standard rule for termination of employment, how long can COBRA coverage generally continue?
choices: 18 months
24 months
36 months
12 months
rationale: Correct — the standard maximum COBRA period after termination of employment is 18 months.
Wrong — 24 months is not the general standard for job loss; it is not the maximum here.
Wrong — 36 months applies to qualifying events such as divorce or the death of the covered employee, not a layoff.
Wrong — 12 months is shorter than the standard maximum for termination of employment.
explanation: COBRA: 18 months for termination or reduced hours; 36 months for many other qualifying events, such as divorce or death of the covered employee.

sub: Long-term care insurance and long-term care planning (individual and group)
q: A client wants a long-term care policy that pays when she needs help with daily living. Under the federal tax definition of a qualified long-term care contract, which standard is used to trigger benefits?
choices: A finding that she requires skilled nursing care at a facility
Inability to perform at least two of six activities of daily living for at least 90 days, or severe cognitive impairment
Any hospitalization lasting longer than 30 days
A physician's statement that she will need care for more than one year
rationale: Wrong — the trigger is not limited to skilled facility care; home and community care also qualify.
Correct — the federal standard uses a two-of-six ADL test (for at least 90 days) or severe cognitive impairment to trigger benefits.
Wrong — hospitalization length is not the federal benefit trigger for long-term care.
Wrong — a physician's prognosis is not the federal test; the test is based on functional ability or cognition.
explanation: Qualified LTC contracts are triggered by inability to perform at least two of six ADLs for 90 days, or severe cognitive impairment.

sub: Long-term care insurance and long-term care planning (individual and group)
q: A 58-year-old client wants to protect her assets from Medicaid spend-down if she later needs long-term care. She is considering a partnership-qualified long-term care policy. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: Partnership policies pay benefits only in a nursing facility, never at home
Partnership policies require the insured to be on Medicaid before benefits start
Partnership policies let the insured keep assets in an amount equal to benefits paid, on a dollar-for-dollar basis, when she later applies for Medicaid in a participating state
Partnership policies eliminate the Medicaid look-back period entirely
rationale: Wrong — partnership policies can cover home and community care as well as facility care.
Wrong — partnership benefits are paid by the insurer, not by Medicaid, and the insured does not need to be on Medicaid first.
Correct — in participating states, assets are protected dollar-for-dollar relative to benefits paid under a qualifying partnership policy.
Wrong — the Medicaid look-back still applies; the partnership benefit works through asset protection, not by removing the look-back.
explanation: Partnership programs protect assets dollar-for-dollar against benefits paid, in states that participate. The Medicaid look-back still applies.

q: An employer provides group term life insurance of $300,000 to an employee. Under the tax rules for group-term life, which statement is correct?
choices: Coverage up to $300,000 is always tax-free to the employee
The employee must pay tax only when the policy pays a death benefit
The entire premium is always taxable to the employee as wages
The cost of employer-paid group term coverage above $50,000 is imputed income to the employee, based on an age-based cost table
rationale: Wrong — coverage above $50,000 creates imputed income each year, so it is not fully tax-free.
Wrong — the tax on imputed income is recognized each year the coverage is provided, not at death.
Wrong — the first $50,000 of group-term coverage is excluded from income; the taxable amount is the excess only.
Correct — the cost of coverage above $50,000 is imputed as income, measured using the IRS age-based cost table.
explanation: Section 79: the first $50,000 of group-term coverage is excluded; the cost of coverage above that is imputed income each year.

q: Three partners own equal shares of a business and want a cross-purchase buy-sell agreement funded with life insurance. How many policies are needed in total so that each partner is insured for the other two?
rationale: Correct — with a cross-purchase plan, each of the three owners holds a policy on each of the other two, or three times two, which is six policies.
Wrong — nine would require an extra set of policies that the cross-purchase design does not need.
Wrong — two policies would leave one partner's interest unfunded in a three-owner structure.
Wrong — three policies would insure each partner only once, not each partner for the other two.
explanation: Cross-purchase plans need n × (n - 1) policies. For three owners, that is 3 × 2 = 6.

q: A client's homeowners policy excludes flood damage. Her home is in a designated flood zone. Which action best addresses this gap?
choices: Rely on the umbrella liability policy to cover flood losses
Add a separate flood insurance policy, such as one from the National Flood Insurance Program or a private carrier
Assume the mortgage lender will cover the loss
Increase her personal property limit in the homeowners policy
rationale: Wrong — an umbrella policy does not insure her own property against flood; it responds to liability claims.
Correct — flood is typically excluded from homeowners policies and requires separate coverage such as NFIP or private flood insurance.
Wrong — a lender does not pay the homeowner's losses; the lender's interest is protected by a required insurance requirement.
Wrong — raising the personal property limit does not add flood coverage, which remains excluded.
explanation: Flood and earthquake are standard exclusions in homeowners policies. Separate coverage is needed, and lenders often require it in designated flood zones.

q: A wealthy client wants to keep the death benefit of a $5 million life policy out of his taxable estate. He plans to have an irrevocable life insurance trust own the policy. Which timing rule is most important?
choices: The trust must be established only after the client reaches age 70
The trust must hold the policy for exactly one year before any premium is paid
If he transfers an existing policy to the trust and dies within three years, the proceeds can still be included in his estate
The policy must be owned by the client for at least ten years before the trust can acquire it
rationale: Wrong — there is no age-70 requirement for an ILIT to hold life insurance.
Wrong — the one-year rule does not govern ILIT premium payments or ownership timing.
Correct — a transfer of an existing life policy within three years of death can pull the proceeds back into the estate, so the three-year rule drives the planning.
Wrong — the rule is about a three-year window from transfer to death, not a ten-year ownership period.
explanation: Under IRC §2035, proceeds of an existing policy transferred within three years of death can be pulled back into the estate. Having the ILIT apply for and own a new policy from the start avoids that transfer issue.
